topic: How OpenAI's Codex Mac agent observes and controls the Mac, and what agents can build for UI testing on macOS 26/27
corpus: A five-backend Dossier panel (Claude local, Perplexity Sonar Deep Research, Gemini Deep Research max, OpenAI gpt-5.6; one Codex-CLI member failed at argv parsing). Four members produced reports, read in full. Anchored by first-party inspection of the machine the page was written on, and one independent web check to settle a cross-backend disagreement. Members disagreed on several points; where they did, the disagreement is carried onto the page rather than resolved silently.

claims.text: Codex's computer-use engine imports the full AXUIElement read and write surface plus ScreenCaptureKit, and imports zero synthetic-event APIs — no CGEventPost, no CGEventCreateMouseEvent, no IOHIDPostEvent. It does not move the pointer or type; it messages the target process directly.
claims.support: Binary import inspection of SkyComputerUseService on this machine; corroborated by all four panel members.
claims.scope: The Electron host's import table is not evidence either way because it calls through an objc-js bridge at runtime; this claim is about the SkyComputerUseService binary specifically.

claims.text: Because an accessibility action is inter-process message to the target, not an event in the shared input stream, Codex can press, toggle and set values on windows that are not frontmost and never steals focus — which is exactly what 'parallel cursors that don't foreground apps' describes.
claims.support: Two control planes established across members; MacStories first-hand account of non-foregrounding parallel operation.
claims.scope: The visible on-screen cursor is a drawn overlay for legibility; there is one real pointer.

claims.text: Codex does not see through the lock screen. While the session is genuinely locked, every real app returns cgWindowNotFound and only loginwindow is reachable. The capability is a real session unlock: a root SecurityAgent plugin participates in the unlock authorization, blanks the displays, acts on a normally-unlocked session, and relocks.
claims.support: First-party logs in openai/codex#26743 (CGSSessionScreenIsLocked=1; only loginwindow responds); the rewritten system.login.screensaver rule present on this machine.
claims.scope: Perplexity inferred the plugin operates through the lock via AX on the lock-screen UI; the better-evidenced reading, from the logs, is unlock-act-relock.

claims.text: On this machine, /Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins/CodexComputerUseAuthorizationPlugin.bundle is installed as root, and the system.login.screensaver authorization rule has been rewritten from Apple's default authenticate-session-owner-or-admin to a rule that runs OpenAI's mechanism first.
claims.support: Direct read of the authorizationdb rule and the plugin bundle on this machine; rule contents corroborated in openai/codex#29616.
claims.scope: This is machine state on one Mac with Codex computer-use enabled, not a claim about every install.

claims.text: Removing the Codex app does not revert the lock-screen rule. The authorization database is system state separate from the app bundle; the default must be restored deliberately with security authorizationdb write.
claims.support: All four members concur; precedent tools (XCreds) ship an explicit rights backup precisely because macOS restores nothing for you.
claims.scope: Reversion command is a single line; stated in the methods note.

claims.text: Third-party SecurityAgent authorization plugins are an established, sanctioned pattern — Jamf Connect, XCreds, Cisco Duo and Apple's own Platform SSO all participate in login or unlock. What is unusual is a consumer AI agent using one on the unlock rule to enable unattended operation.
claims.support: Named precedents with vendor documentation across three members.
claims.scope: Structurally consistent with Apple's design; the novelty is the use case, not the mechanism.

claims.text: The lock-screen broker socket at /tmp/com.openai.sky.CUAService/LockScreenLoginAuthorization.sock is world-writable (0666), but application-level default-deny mitigates it: every unauthenticated request — including a silent connect — returns DENY.
claims.support: Direct benign probe on this machine returned DENY to a silent connect and to HTTP/JSON requests; gpt-5.6 independently reasoned a world-writable socket is not exploitable if the server authenticates peers.
claims.scope: This establishes fail-closed behaviour against an unauthenticated peer. It does not establish whether the authentication token is forgeable, which was not tested.

claims.text: Because server-delivered JavaScript runs against an Objective-C bridge, the client's effective native capability is chosen by the server at runtime, not fixed by its binary. Import-table and entitlement analysis establishes what the host could do, not what a given turn did.
claims.support: The objc-js bridge, cua_node/node_repl and server-delivered kernel.js are present on this machine; all four members reach the same auditability conclusion; comparable public designs are Cloudflare Code Mode and Anthropic's code-execution-with-MCP.
claims.scope: Whether the bridge is capability-allowlisted or unrestricted could not be established from public sources; it is the highest-value open question.

claims.text: There is no native getComputedStyle for third-party macOS apps. Every richer mechanism — View Debugger transport, MTLCaptureManager, CoreText interposition, PDF re-render — requires code injection into the target, which hardened runtime and Library Validation block. AX geometry plus pixels is the ceiling for apps you do not own.
claims.support: Unanimous across all four members with per-mechanism analysis.
claims.scope: Inverts entirely for your own apps.

claims.text: The durable build for your own apps is a debug-only in-process reflector: a #if DEBUG endpoint that serialises the view/layer hierarchy with resolved colours, fonts, corner radius, constraints and Core Animation model/presentation values — a genuine computed-style analogue, no private API, no notarisation risk.
claims.support: Both best-sourced members independently recommend this as the build; Claude names it days-not-weeks, gpt-5.6 gives a concrete schema.
claims.scope: Applies to owned apps; foreign apps stay AX-plus-pixels.

claims.text: The Library-Validation tightening that closes third-party injection is already biting a first-party vendor: OpenAI's own SecurityAgent helper is rejected on macOS 26.5 with 'mapping process is a platform binary, but mapped file is not'.
claims.support: openai/codex#24013 log excerpt; two members cite the same rejection class.
claims.scope: Whether Apple closes this path deliberately or #24013 is a regression determines whether locked-use survives macOS 27.

claims.text: There is no native macOS analogue to CDP's setVirtualTimePolicy. Core Animation timing runs in the out-of-process render server on the system clock, with no supported hook to slave it to a test clock. Determinism must be engineered from settle-signals plus per-step state hashing, not enforced by the OS.
claims.support: Unanimous; each member ranks the honesty of the available settle signals.
claims.scope: In-process CALayer.speed control is available for your own apps only.

claims.text: The accessibility tree is negotiated, not fixed: Electron and Chromium build no full tree until a client sets AXManualAccessibility or AXEnhancedUserInterface, the first walk often returns empty, and setting the flag is detectable by the app and changes its performance — an observer effect that is a genuine validity threat for an e2e suite.
claims.support: All four members; Electron's own app.setAccessibilitySupportEnabled reports AT presence to app code.
claims.scope: An AX-driven suite is measuring the app in its assistive-technology configuration, not the one a human runs — state this in any methodology.

claims.text: Members disagreed on whether Electron/Chromium honour AX actions on unfocused windows: one reported they discard AXPress when out of focus and require activation, the others that they honour it after tree activation. The confound is lazy-tree materialisation — an unactivated tree looks like a refusal.
claims.support: Gemini reports discard-when-unfocused; Claude and gpt-5.6 report honour-after-activation.
claims.scope: Carried as stated uncertainty; the practical answer is toolkit- and activation-dependent.

claims.text: Background and occluded window capture can return stale pixels, and a stale frame looks identical to a correct one. ScreenCaptureKit exposes SCFrameStatus.idle and dirty rects to detect no-new-pixels, but off-screen windows may emit complete frames only when there is mouse movement on their display — a background capture on an idle machine can receive nothing.
claims.support: Apple's SCFrameStatus documentation; the mouse-movement constraint is from Apple's ScreenCaptureKit developer-forum guidance via Claude.
claims.scope: The honest freshness assertion is three-way agreement between semantic AX state, compositor frame metadata, and (for owned apps) a render revision.

claims.text: Parallelism is hardware-bound: Apple silicon enforces a cap of two concurrent macOS guests per host via the kernel counter hv_apple_isa_vm_quota, returning VZErrorVirtualMachineLimitExceeded on the third. It still holds in the macOS 27 cycle, applies only to macOS guests, and lifts only by disabling SIP.
claims.support: Independent web check confirming the named kernel counter and error, with a WWDC26 Virtualization Q&A in the macOS 27 cycle; two members asserted the cap.
claims.scope: gpt-5.6 declined to confirm the number for 26/27 from public API docs; the independent check resolves it toward two. Meaningful parallel macOS UI testing is a hardware-purchase decision, not a software one.

claims.text: Declared automation contracts are not a general escape from pixels: App Intents has no third-party programmatic invocation API — the sanctioned callers are Shortcuts, Spotlight and Siri — AppleScript coverage is declining and inconsistent, and URL schemes are write-only. AX remains the only broad cross-application semantic surface, which is why a general Mac agent must fall back to it.
claims.support: All four members; the shortcuts CLI is the only practical intent escape hatch and it is bounded by adoption.
claims.scope: No public evidence establishes that Codex routes through intents before AX; observed behaviour points to AX-first with Apple Events as fallback.

claims.text: One member uniquely reported the node_repl runtime leaking up to 271 unreaped helper processes consuming 10-13 GB, and another uniquely reported a 17.5-minute lock-screen stall versus ~73ms after removing the rule. Each is a single-member finding, attributed rather than treated as corroborated.
claims.support: Zombie-process leak from Gemini via openai/codex#37672; the unlock stall from Claude via openai/codex#29616.
claims.scope: Support is counted in independent domains; these are one member each and are labelled as such on the page.

claims.text: Engagement is not comprehension: a scroll-driven cited page of this kind is measured to buy attention and perceived clarity, not understanding. This page claims neither for itself.
claims.support: Methods-note claim about the page itself, carried from the skill's own evidence base.
claims.scope: Stated so the page does not overclaim its own format.
